title: Losing muscle after 50: why protein and strength training matter
intro: Ever found it hard to get up from a low chair or lift a bag of rice? That may be a sign your muscle is decreasing. This is common as we age, but it is not something we just have to accept. With enough protein and light strength training, you can protect your muscle.

sections.h: What happens to muscle as we age
sections.p: After our 30s, muscle slowly decreases if we don't use it. After 50, the process can speed up. Doctors call this loss of muscle and strength sarcopenia. Signs include walking more slowly, getting tired quickly climbing stairs, and struggling to open bottle caps.

sections.h: Why muscle matters for weight, sugar and falls
sections.p: Muscle is where the body uses and stores sugar. The more active muscle you have, the easier it is for the body to manage blood sugar. Muscle also helps the body use energy even at rest. Most importantly, strong leg muscles lower the risk of falling. When we lose weight without protecting muscle, some of what we lose may be muscle, not just fat.

sections.h: How much protein: a simple estimate
sections.p: Many experts suggest healthy older adults take an estimated 1.0 to 1.2 g of protein per kg of body weight per day. Example: if you weigh 65 kg, the estimated target is 65 to 78 g a day. This is only an estimate, and people with kidney disease need to follow their doctor's advice. Easy way: have a palm-sized protein source at every main meal. Estimated protein: 1 egg about 6 g, a palm-sized piece of chicken or fish about 20 to 25 g, a medium piece of tofu about 8 to 10 g, a glass of low-fat milk about 8 g, a bowl of dhal about 7 to 9 g.

At the mamak: add an egg to your roti canai, or choose roti telur with dhal. At the nasi campur stall: take a piece of fish or chicken, one vegetable dish, and just enough rice. Bihun goreng for breakfast? Add a fried egg. For a light dinner, tofu, tempeh, ikan bilis or chicken soup also help. Spread your protein through the day, not all at dinner.

Strength training means making your muscles work against a load. The load can be your own body weight, a filled water bottle or a small bag of rice. Examples: sit-to-stand from a chair, wall push-ups, heel raises while holding on, and lifting water bottles to shoulder level. Do it 2 to 3 times a week, with a rest day in between. Start light, add a little at a time.

action: Check your plate today: is there palm-sized protein at breakfast, lunch and dinner?
Add an egg or a piece of tofu to one meal that is usually low in protein.
Do 10 sit-to-stands from a chair and 10 wall push-ups, 2 times this week.
Fill 2 water bottles of 500 ml and use them as 'dumbbells' to lift your arms to the front and to the side.
doctor: See a doctor first before adding a lot of protein if you have kidney disease, gout or your doctor has told you to limit protein. Also see a doctor if you are losing weight for no reason, getting weaker quickly, or falling often. Before starting strength training, discuss with your doctor if you have heart disease, uncontrolled blood pressure, or eye problems such as retina problems from diabetes. Do not change your medicine on your own.

faq.q: I'm already old. Can I still build muscle?
faq.a: Yes. Studies show people aged 60, 70 and even 80 can still gain strength when they do strength training consistently. Start slowly, and be patient. Strength usually improves within a few weeks.

faq.q: If I don't eat much meat, how can I get enough protein?
faq.a: There are many other choices: eggs, tofu, tempeh, dhal, chickpeas, milk, yogurt and fish. Combine these sources through the day. For example, eggs for breakfast, fish for lunch, tofu and vegetables for dinner.

faq.q: Do I need to lift heavy weights?
faq.a: No need. To start, your own body weight and water bottles are enough. The guide is that the last repetition feels quite challenging, but you can still do it with proper form and without joint pain.
